Q1.text: Neural IR models had mostly been studied in homogeneous, narrow settings, limiting insight into their out-of-distribution generalization.
It was unclear how well trained neural retrieval models perform on other text domains or retrieval tasks, and how different approach types (sparse vs dense) generalize out of distribution.

Q2.text: Prior work commonly trains and evaluates neural retrievers on the same large dataset (e.g. NQ, MS MARCO), which does not reveal how they perform elsewhere.
Building large training corpora is time-consuming and expensive, so many retrieval systems are deployed zero-shot with no target-domain training data.

Q3.text: Existing retrieval benchmarks such as MultiReQA and KILT were narrower: they focused on a single task type or domain and did not evaluate zero-shot generalization in depth.
MultiReQA covers only question-answering, is mostly Wikipedia-based (5 of 8 datasets), and 6 of 8 tasks have fewer than 100k candidate sentences.
KILT covers five knowledge-intensive tasks (eleven datasets) but retrieves only from Wikipedia and treats retrieval as a secondary component rather than the primary task.

Q4.text: The authors built BEIR, a benchmark of 18 zero-shot retrieval datasets spanning 9 heterogeneous tasks and domains.
They released an open-source Python package (installable via pip) that converts datasets into a standardized corpus/queries/qrels format and wraps multiple retrieval libraries for evaluation.
They evaluated ten retrieval systems spanning five architecture families (lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, re-ranking) on the benchmark.
They conducted a targeted bias study manually re-annotating 980 query-document pairs in TREC-COVID to measure the impact of lexical annotation bias.

Q5.text: Datasets were selected using four criteria: diverse tasks, diverse domains, sufficient task difficulty, and diverse annotation strategies.

nDCG@10 was chosen as the single primary metric because rank-unaware metrics (Precision/Recall) and binary rank-aware metrics (MRR/MAP) cannot properly evaluate datasets with graded relevance judgements.
Documents were truncated to the first 512 word pieces for all neural models due to transformer input-length limits.

Q6.text: A zero-shot comparison of 10 models across 18 datasets plus in-domain MS MARCO reporting nDCG@10 for each model-dataset pair.
A latency and index-size study on a randomly sampled 1-million-document subset of DBPedia, measured on both CPU and GPU.
A manual re-annotation study on TREC-COVID measuring Hole@10 and nDCG@10 before and after adding missing relevance judgements.
An ablation comparing cosine-similarity vs. dot-product SBERT models (otherwise identically trained) on TREC-COVID, Signal-1M(RT), and FEVER.

Q7.text: The re-ranking model BM25+CE had the best average zero-shot performance vs. BM25 (+11%) and outperformed BM25 on 16 of 18 datasets.
The late-interaction model ColBERT outperformed BM25 on 9 of 18 datasets, with an average performance of +2.5% vs. BM25.
docT5query (sparse) outperformed BM25 on 11 of 18 datasets while remaining competitive elsewhere, with average +1.6% vs. BM25.
Dense/sparse models such as DeepCT (-27.9%), SPARTA (-20.3%), and DPR (-47.7%) had substantially negative average performance relative to BM25.

Q8.text: In-domain performance on MS MARCO does not predict a model's zero-shot generalization performance across BEIR's 18 datasets.

There is a trade-off between generalization performance and computational cost: the best-generalizing model types (re-ranking, late-interaction) are also the slowest at inference (>350ms) while dense retrievers are 20-30x faster.

Manual re-annotation of TREC-COVID measurably raised nDCG@10 for every tested system, with the largest gains for systems that had high Hole@10 rates (e.g. ANCE improved from 0.654 to 0.735, a 6.7-point gain over BM25).
BEIR datasets can carry a lexical annotation bias, since the annotation candidate pools were often built using lexical retrieval systems, disadvantaging non-lexical models.

Q9.text: The benchmark covers English-only datasets; multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval were not evaluated.
The benchmark does not integrate non-textual relevance signals such as PageRank, recency, authority score, or click-through rate.
Because all neural models truncated documents to the first 512 word pieces, the reported comparisons do not establish how these models would compare on full, untruncated long documents.

Q10.text: The primary contribution is a heterogeneous, 18-dataset, 9-task zero-shot benchmark (BEIR) for evaluating IR model generalization.
A second contribution is a comparative zero-shot evaluation of 10 retrieval architectures, showing no single approach dominates and that in-domain performance does not predict generalization.
A third contribution is an analysis of annotation selection bias via manual TREC-COVID re-annotation, showing non-lexical approaches are disadvantaged by lexically-biased annotation pools.
The authors released BEIR as a documented, extensible open-source package integrating diverse retrieval systems and datasets.

Q11.text: The benchmark is English-only; the authors note multilingual datasets should be added in future work.
The benchmark focuses on pure textual search and does not include long-document retrieval or multi-field retrieval (e.g. title, abstract, body, authors as separate fields).
No error bars or repeated-run variance are reported, because most evaluated models are pre-trained checkpoints that the authors could not feasibly retrain.
Task-specific specialized models were not evaluated and are noted as not necessarily needing to generalize across all tasks the way BEIR's generalist models must.

Q12.text: BEIR is a 18-dataset, 9-task, zero-shot benchmark showing that no single IR model architecture wins everywhere, and that in-domain accuracy does not predict out-of-domain generalization.
Re-ranking and late-interaction models generalize best but are the most computationally expensive; BM25 remains a strong, cheap baseline.
Many retrieval benchmark annotations carry a lexical bias that can understate the true performance of non-lexical (e.g. dense) retrieval systems.
